opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and I think of them less as competitors and more as different tools that sit at different points on a spectrum of trade-offs.

NeRFs and 3D Gaussian splats are both scene reconstruction techniques. You take sensor data your fleet has already collected, camera images and often lidar, and build a 3D representation of that scene that you can re-render from new viewpoints. That matters for simulation, because if your planner decides to do something slightly different than the logged vehicle did, say it nudges over half a lane, you need to show it what the cameras and lidar would have seen from that new position. NeRFs showed this was possible with high fidelity. Gaussian splats have become very attractive because they're explicit, much faster to render, and easier to edit. You can move objects around, remove them, insert new ones, and still hit real-time or near-real-time rates, which matters at scale.

But reconstruction has a fundamental limitation: it's anchored to what you observed. If you drift too far from the original trajectory, you start seeing regions you never captured, and quality degrades. Artifacts, holes, blurry geometry. You also can't easily get scenarios that never happened: different weather, different times of day, new agents behaving in new ways, rare long-tail events.

That's where generative models, diffusion in particular, come in. They've learned strong priors about what the world looks like, so they can fill in unobserved regions, fix reconstruction artifacts, and change appearance, turning a sunny day into rain or night. More ambitiously, they can generate entirely new scenarios that are realistic but never logged. And it isn't only sensor appearance; diffusion has been very effective for generating agent behaviors and whole traffic scenes, which is just as important for a useful simulator.

So the picture I find compelling is a hybrid. Use reconstruction, Gaussian splats being a strong choice right now, to get a grounded, geometrically consistent, controllable representation of real scenes. Then layer generative models on top to enhance fidelity, extrapolate beyond the observed data, and create diversity and novel situations. Reconstruction gives you realism and consistency tied to the real world; generation gives you coverage and the ability to imagine. You really want both.

The open challenges are in making that combination consistent across time and across sensors, so cameras and lidar agree with each other and with the 3D world, and making it efficient enough to run millions of miles of simulation. Ultimately, the question for any simulator is whether it's realistic enough that your evaluation results transfer to the real world. That's the bar we hold all of these techniques to.

r002.rationale: It says Gaussian splats are easier to edit and explicitly describes moving, removing, and inserting objects, so it does not communicate that these methods do not readily support modifying the environment.

r003.rationale: It says diffusion models can generate realistic scenarios that were never logged, including new agent behaviors and traffic scenes.

r004.rationale: It discusses generating novel scenarios and changing appearance, but does not raise how to condition a simulation on a specific real-world location.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so that's a great question, and I think the honest answer is that they each solve a different part of the problem, and the interesting work right now is in how you stitch them together.

If you step back, what we want from a simulator is something that's realistic, that's controllable, and that's fast enough that you can run it at scale against the full stack, including the perception system. And historically, no single technique gives you all three.

So the first piece is reconstruction. We have an enormous amount of logged data from the fleet, and the most direct way to get a realistic environment is to rebuild the world from what the cars actually saw. That's where neural rendering comes in. NeRFs were the first big step there, because they showed you could take camera and lidar data and get a volumetric representation that you can re-render from novel viewpoints. The problem with NeRFs for our use case was really speed, and to some degree how hard they were to edit. You'd get a beautiful scene, but rendering it was slow enough that running closed-loop simulation with the real perception stack on top was painful.

3D Gaussian splats, to me, are kind of the practical successor. You get similar or better visual quality, but now it's an explicit representation, a set of primitives, and that buys you two things. One, you can rasterize it very fast, so you're suddenly in the regime where closed-loop simulation at scale is realistic. And two, because it's explicit, it's much easier to manipulate. You can separate the static background from dynamic actors, you can move a vehicle, you can remove a pedestrian, you can compose scenes out of pieces that came from different logs. So for us, splats have become the workhorse for the "reconstruct the world and then perturb it" style of simulation.

But reconstruction has a fundamental limitation, which is that it only knows about what you observed. If the car drove down the road and the camera never saw the far side of a parked truck, the reconstruction has a hole there. If you want to put the ego vehicle in a lane it never drove in, or push the viewpoint a few meters off the trajectory, the quality degrades. And the whole point of simulation is to go to places the fleet didn't go, because that's where the rare and dangerous stuff lives.

That's where the diffusion models and generative models more broadly come in. They've learned a prior over what the world looks like, so they can fill in the gaps. You can use them to inpaint missing regions in a reconstruction, to make a novel view look plausible where the splat is breaking down, to change weather or lighting on a scene you captured in daylight. And at the far end, you can generate entirely new scenarios from scratch, conditioned on a map or a layout or a text description. So they extend the coverage of what you can simulate well beyond what you've logged.

The flip side is that generative models have their own weaknesses. They're not inherently 3D consistent, they can hallucinate, and they're expensive, especially if you're trying to generate video over time with multiple cameras and keep everything coherent. So you don't want to rely on them for everything.

So the way I think about it is roughly a spectrum. Reconstruction, and splats in particular, give you grounding, geometric consistency, and speed, anchored to real data. Diffusion gives you coverage and controllability where the data runs out. And the systems that are working best right now are hybrids, where the explicit 3D representation acts as a scaffold and the generative model either refines the rendering or fills in what the scaffold can't support. You get something that's consistent across frames and across cameras, because the geometry is doing that work, but still photorealistic in regions you never actually observed.

And I'd add one more thing, which is that the sensor realism is only half of simulation. The other half is behavior, how the other agents react to you. And there, generative models are also playing a growing role, not for pixels but for trajectories. So the same philosophy applies: you ground in real logged behavior, and you use learned models to extrapolate into the interactions you haven't seen. The sensor side and the behavior side need to come together for the simulator to actually be useful for evaluating and training the driver.

astra-6.text:
I think they address different parts of the problem. NeRFs and 3D Gaussian splats give you a way to reconstruct a scene from observations and render it from new viewpoints. For driving simulation, that’s valuable because you want to take a situation you’ve captured and see what happens when the vehicle follows a different trajectory. Gaussian splats are particularly attractive for rendering efficiently.

Diffusion models bring a complementary capability: generating variation. Reconstruction gives you a particular scene, but you want to explore different conditions and potentially different configurations of that scene. Generative models can help expand that space.

The challenge is making all of this consistent and controllable. A scene can look convincing in an image and still be wrong geometrically, or change inconsistently over time. In a driving simulation, those errors matter. You need the sensor observations, the underlying geometry, and the behavior of other agents to agree. So I see these techniques coming together, with reconstruction providing a grounding in observed environments and generative models helping broaden the situations we can test.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they play complementary roles. NeRFs and 3D Gaussian splats give you ways to reconstruct a scene from observations and render it from new viewpoints. That’s useful for taking a real driving log and turning it into an environment where you can move the simulated vehicle around. Gaussian splats are particularly attractive for rendering efficiently.

Diffusion models bring a generative capability. Reconstruction alone doesn’t necessarily tell you what should appear in an area you haven’t observed, or how to create a different version of a scene. Generative models can help fill those gaps and introduce variation.

The challenge is making all of that consistent. For driving simulation, a scene can’t just look plausible in a single image. It needs to remain coherent across viewpoints, across cameras, and over time, and respond appropriately as the vehicle moves. So I see reconstruction providing the grounding in the real world, with generative models expanding the range of situations we can simulate.
